question: What happens to the body's energy and protein needs after surgery?

options.A: They remain exactly the same as pre-surgery levels
options.B: They decrease because the patient is resting in bed
options.C: They increase due to tissue trauma and healing
options.D: They stop completely until solid food is tolerated

explanation: Great job! Surgery causes physical stress, so the body needs extra energy and protein to heal the tissues properly. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h1)

question: Why is checking for malnutrition important before a patient goes for surgery?

options.A: It shortens the time the patient spends in the recovery room
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for any intravenous fluids
options.C: It ensures the patient will never feel nauseated after waking up
options.D: It helps the body withstand surgical stress and prevents complications

explanation: Spot on! Well-nourished patients handle the stress of an operation much better and have a lower risk of infections. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h1)

question: Which blood test is commonly checked to assess a patient's nutrition before surgery?
explanation: You got it! Serum albumin is a classic protein marker we use to check a surgical patient's nutritional reserves. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h2)

question: Why might a patient be given a carbohydrate drink up to two hours before surgery?

options.A: To replace the need for intravenous fluids during the operation
options.B: To reduce insulin resistance and postoperative discomfort
options.C: To prevent the patient from experiencing surgical site infections
options.D: To completely fill the stomach so the patient feels full

explanation: Correct! Giving carbs before surgery helps calm fasting stress, keeps insulin working well, and cuts down on post-surgery nausea. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h2)

question: Which hormones are mainly responsible for breaking down fat and muscle during the stress of surgery?
explanation: Well done! Stress hormones like cortisol and glucagon shoot up during surgery to quickly mobilize energy for the body. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h3)

question: Why is getting enough protein so crucial during the body's recovery phase after surgery?

options.A: It acts as a mild pain reliever for the surgical wound
options.B: It prevents the patient from experiencing low blood pressure
options.C: It stops the endocrine system from releasing stress hormones
options.D: It provides the amino acids needed to rebuild broken down muscle and repair incisions

explanation: Right! Protein supplies the building blocks (amino acids) needed to close wounds and rebuild tissues after the body has broken them down. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h3)

question: When do modern recovery guidelines generally suggest starting food by mouth after surgery?

options.A: Only after 48 hours of complete fasting
options.B: Within hours of waking from anesthesia
options.C: After waiting for active bowel sounds
options.D: Only after the patient passes flatus

explanation: Spot on! Feeding patients early is safe and actually helps their bowels wake up faster than starving them for days. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h4)

question: A patient eating a full liquid diet after surgery suddenly gets severe stomach cramps and vomits. What should you do first?

options.A: Immediately upgrade the diet to solid foods
options.B: Encourage the patient to finish the meal quickly
options.C: Document the findings and ignore the symptoms
options.D: Pause the feeding and notify the surgical team

explanation: Correct! Cramping and vomiting mean the gut isn't ready yet. We need to stop the feeding and let the doctor know. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h4)

question: Why is feeding through the gut (enteral nutrition) usually preferred over drips (parenteral nutrition) for surgical patients?

options.A: It preserves gut immune function and carries fewer infectious risks
options.B: It is absorbed much faster than intravenous fluids
options.C: It bypasses the digestive system entirely
options.D: It can be administered without any medical equipment

explanation: You got it! Using the natural digestive tract keeps the gut healthy and avoids the high infection risks that come with central lines. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h5)

question: When is total parenteral nutrition (feeding directly into the veins) specifically needed?

options.A: When the gastrointestinal tract is completely non-functional or obstructed
options.B: When the patient simply dislikes the taste of hospital food
options.C: When the patient is able to swallow clear liquids
options.D: When the surgery only involved a minor skin biopsy

explanation: Spot on! We only use IV nutrition when the gut cannot work or is blocked, since it bypasses the digestive system completely. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h5)

question: What is dumping syndrome?

options.A: An allergic reaction to intravenous protein solutions
options.B: Rapid emptying of stomach contents into the small intestine causing dizziness and cramps
options.C: The inability of the kidneys to filter waste products after major surgery
options.D: The total stoppage of bowel movements for over a week

explanation: Well done! Dumping syndrome happens when food rushes too fast from a smaller stomach into the small intestine, making the patient feel dizzy and cramped. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h6)

question: Why are bariatric (weight-loss) surgery patients told not to drink fluids at the same time they eat solid meals?

options.A: To prevent the stomach from overfilling and to avoid triggering dumping syndrome
options.B: To prevent the absorption of any vitamins or minerals
options.C: To make digestion take as long as humanly possible
options.D: To ensure they lose as much water weight as possible

explanation: Correct! Drinking water with meals washes the food through a tiny stomach pouch too quickly, causing discomfort and cramping. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h6)

question: Which vitamin is especially important for building collagen during long-term wound healing?
explanation: You nailed it! Vitamin C is key for making collagen, which acts like glue to heal surgical cuts. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h7)

question: Why does recovery from surgery continue for weeks or months after the skin stitches are removed?

options.A: Patients are usually restricted to liquid diets for six months
options.B: Deep internal tissues take weeks to months to regain full tensile strength
options.C: External healing is just a cosmetic illusion with no internal progress
options.D: The body stops absorbing any nutrients once the skin closes

explanation: Spot on! Even though the outside skin looks fine, the deeper muscles and tissues take much longer to get their full strength back. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h7)

question: What is a very common side effect of post-surgical pain medications that ruins a patient's appetite?
explanation: Right! Pain medicines like opioids slow down the bowels, causing stubborn constipation that kills appetite and brings on nausea. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h8)

question: A postoperative patient refuses to eat because food always brings severe belly pain and nausea. What is your best nursing action?

options.A: Administer prescribed pain and anti-nausea medications thirty minutes before the next meal
options.B: Remove all food trays permanently and start total parenteral nutrition
options.C: Force the patient to finish the entire meal tray immediately
options.D: Tell the patient that eating is mandatory for legal discharge

explanation: Brilliant! Managing pain and nausea before mealtime makes eating comfortable so the patient can actually get their nutrition. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T009#GNS227_U7_T009_h8)
